nameStory: This moth earned its "bristly cutworm" name from its caterpillar stage, which has a bristly, spiky appearance and feeds at night by cutting through plant stems at ground level. The "kidney-spotted minor" name comes from the distinctive kidney-shaped spots on the forewings, while "minor" refers to its relatively small size compared to other cutworm moths.
description: The Bristly Cutworm Moth is a medium-sized brown moth that's active from late spring through fall across New England. Like other members of the cutworm moth family (Noctuidae), it has a sturdy build with mottled brown and gray wings that help it blend perfectly with tree bark during the day. The forewings typically show distinctive kidney-shaped spots and wavy lines, while the hindwings are usually paler. These moths have a wingspan of about 1-1.5 inches and thick, fuzzy bodies typical of night-flying moths.

idTips.label: Kidney-shaped wing spots
idTips.description: Look for distinctive kidney or bean-shaped spots (called reniform spots) on each forewing - they're usually outlined in pale scales and are the moth's most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Mottled brown coloration
idTips.description: Wings have a complex pattern of browns, grays, and sometimes rusty tones that feel rough and scaly to the touch, like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Wavy cross-lines
idTips.description: Forewings show zigzag or wavy lines running across the wing surface, often appearing as lighter or darker bands against the mottled background

idTips.label: Thick, fuzzy body
idTips.description: The body feels soft and woolly when gently touched, much like a cotton ball, and is proportionally thick compared to the wing span

idTips.label: Pale hindwings
idTips.description: The back wings are noticeably lighter than the patterned forewings, often appearing almost white or very pale gray with minimal markings

habitat: Bristly Cutworm Moths can be found throughout New England's varied landscapes, from suburban gardens and agricultural fields to forest edges and meadows. They're particularly common in areas with mixed vegetation where their caterpillars can feed on grasses, weeds, and crop plants. You'll often spot adults at porch lights, gas stations, and other artificial light sources during their active season.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May, with the first generation appearing at outdoor lights on warm evenings. Look for fresh moths with crisp wing patterns and bright coloration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when multiple generations overlap. Moths are most active on warm, humid nights and can be found resting on tree bark during the day.
seasonality.fall: The final generation flies through October, with moths appearing more worn and faded. Late-season individuals may look quite different from fresh spring specimens.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active; the species overwinters as pupae in the soil or as young caterpillars, depending on the generation.

funFact: Despite being called a "cutworm" moth, the caterpillars are actually beneficial in many ecosystems because they help aerate soil through their burrowing behavior and serve as important food sources for ground-feeding birds like robins and thrushes who have learned to hunt for them at dawn when they're still active near the surface.
confusionNotes: This moth can easily be confused with other brown cutworm moths in the Noctuidae family, but the kidney-shaped spots are your best bet for identification. Remember: "kidney spots = kidney-spotted minor" - if you see those distinctive bean-shaped marks on the forewings, you've likely found your Bristly Cutworm Moth.
contextualKnowledge: The name "minor" in "kidney-spotted minor" doesn't mean this moth is unimportant, but rather refers to its smaller size compared to "major" cutworm moth species. This European naming convention can be confusing since there are many North American moths that don't follow this size-based naming system.
compareHints: Since this is the only Lacinipolia species in our New England dataset, compare it to other common cutworm moths like the Black Cutworm Moth or Variegated Cutworm Moth. The Bristly Cutworm Moth tends to be more consistently brown with clearer kidney spots, while its relatives often show more contrasting colors or less defined wing patterns. The wavy cross-lines on this species are also typically more pronounced and regular than on similar moths.
